utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, General. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, General. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: I understand you perfectly, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, General, perhaps I could ask you some preliminary questions. First, do you recall giving a statement to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor for this Tribunal in 1997?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: I'll start with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you've testified before this Tribunal on two previous occasions, have you not? First, during the trial of Stanislav Galic in 2002, and then again in 2003, during the trial of Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Both testimonies are correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just over one year ago, you signed a further statement for the Office of the Prosecutor, consolidating elements of your previously-given evidence, with some additional clarifications and observations, and also references to a number of documents; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, have you reviewed that statement and looked at the documents it refers to in preparation for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: I've reviewed all documents presented to me again, and I had a few modifications in pen entered as a final update yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Then just referring to that update yesterday, perhaps I could ask you -- or help you to explain that this way: By way of corrections to that 2009 document, did you, yesterday, sign an updated copy which properly displays the Serbo-Croatian diacritics and incorporates some handwritten changes that you made to the 2009 version, as well as a number of typographical corrections?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct, two corrections with respect to dates on page 3 at items 6 and 7. To re-correct: On item 6, I flew to Zagreb on 6 February, and 7 February 1994 I spoke with General Rose. And at item 7, in the third sentence, the correct date has been entered of the bombing incident at Markale Market in Sarajevo on 5 February. In addition, various abbreviations referring to the Milosevic and the Galic case have been written out in full throughout the document --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in every other regard, is this document you signed yesterday identical to your statement of 2009?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: I checked that, and it's fully identical.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, then, if you were asked the same questions today which gave rise to the evidence contained in this document, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That being the case, then, Your Honours, could I ask that 65 ter 22288, which is the updated amalgamated statement of the general, be marked as a Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. With respect to paragraph 71, which describes incidents in Gorazde, we would object and ask that that be redacted for the same reasons we gave with respect to General Rose. You've already ruled on that, but I wanted to preserve that objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You know the Chamber's position, so I will not repeat our ruling. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1818, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. What I would propose to do now, then, is to read a summary of the written evidence that's just been admitted. The witness, General Adrianus van Baal, served as the chief of staff of the Bosnia and Herzegovina UNPROFOR Command from 24 February 1994 to 28 August 1994. From his pre-tour briefings and his own observations on his arrival, he concluded that the post-Markale Market cease-fire of February 1994 was effectively implemented. At this time, the Serb side wanted peace on the pre-condition of a complete cease-fire and the demilitarisation of Sarajevo and other safe areas. General Van Baal observed an increase in sniping incidents during this cease-fire period. Incidents of sniping of civilians attributed to the Bosnian Serb side were raised with the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and higher levels of the VRS. General Van Baal specifically recalls that tram passengers were the object of sniping. In a meeting in March 1994, General Milovanovic complained to General Van Baal that trams were now operating in Sarajevo and it presented an incorrect impression that there was peace when, in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole, war continued. General Milovanovic said that he would see to it that trams would, therefore, be targeted, and following this meeting, trams were targeted by snipers from the Bosnian Serb side. General Van Baal concluded, from meetings with VRS leaders and observations on the ground, that the VRS leadership retained effective command and control of their forces. The VRS had a functioning communications system, evidenced by, for example, their immediate responses on the ground to threats of NATO air-strikes in August of 1994. Restrictions on freedom of movement were another example, which were dictated at the Main Staff level. During meetings in March 1994 with Mr. Karadzic and the Sarajevo Romanija Corps commander, General Galic, General Van Baal also observed that the accused retained effective command over the military. General Van Baal telephoned Mr. Karadzic when 600 VRS soldiers from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps's Ilijas Brigade surrounded Canadian peacekeepers enforcing the Total Exclusion Zone. Mr. Karadzic told the witness that he would give orders not to shoot, and 20 minutes later the soldiers withdrew. Overnight, the VRS soldiers placed mines under the Canadian APCs. When General Van Baal refused to talk to Mr. Karadzic during a meeting in Pale the following day until the mines had been removed, he watched Mr. Karadzic verbally order General Galic to have those mines removed, and within 20 minutes both the Canadians and the VRS confirmed that the order had been carried out. That's the summary of the written evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And now just to go further, General, with a few additional questions for you, perhaps I could ask you to update your CV for everyone from the time you returned to the Netherlands at the end of August 1994.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: In August 1994, I returned to the Netherlands. And from early October, I served as director of operations for the Royal Air Force and also as deputy commander. Excuse me, not the Air Force, the Royal Dutch Military. And I was subsequently responsible for directing the operational units that were being prepared for deployment in mission areas, and I was also responsible for ensuring logistical support from the Netherlands of the units deployed in Bosnia-Herzegovina Command, including DutchBat in Srebrenica. I observed intensive deterioration of the situation, culminating in the fall of Srebrenica, the return of DutchBat, and especially the worldwide observation of at least 7.000 men and boys that perished in the fall of Srebrenica. Subsequently, in 1996, I became deputy chief of Defence Staff and as such was directly involved in all crisis management operations of the military during that period. I was in close contact with units on the ground in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as in other places, and was able to closely follow the developments and wield influence via the chief of Defence Staff. Subsequently, after four and a half years, I became commander of the Royal Dutch Military, and a year after I assumed this command, the NIOD report at the Dutch Institute for War Documentation was published, reflecting an extensive investigation of the circumstances fall of the Srebrenica enclave and all the consequences thereof. The publication of the report had a major impact on the Dutch government. The Dutch government resigned following the publication of the report and its contents. And for me, as a commander operating without the support of politicians was absolutely impossible at that point. And for the sake of the functioning of the Royal Dutch Military and good relations between the military leadership, the Royal Dutch Military and the political leadership, I believed it was appropriate to make my position available. This happened in April 2002. At the end of 2002, a parliamentary inquiry examined the questions that remained unanswered. One of those questions was whether it was justified that General Van Baal resign from his office, and their conclusion was that this was not necessary and was not rightly so. Next, I accepted a position as reorganiser at the central organisation of the ministry, and I served in that position for one year. Then I entered my final position as inspector general of the Dutch military for three and a half years. And when I turned 60, I resigned from the military and subsequently considered other jobs. I thought I was too young to stop working, and I accepted a wonderful job in September 2007 as chairman of the Executive Board of the Police Academy, and I'm still delighted to have this job. This is my working update. Please note that the three moments in the period when I returned 16 years ago in Bosnia-Herzegovina are still very clear to me, the testimony from General Mladic [as interpreted] -- excuse me, General Mladic and Milosevic and my testimony here today. [In English] Not General Mladic, but General Galic. It's wrong in line 12/09.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. You've just referred to the period 16 years ago in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'll, in a few questions, then, take you back there, if I may, to the time of your arrival to take up office in UNPROFOR in February 1994. Where were you based on your arrival?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I started at the headquarters in Kiseljak, and one of the most important assignments I was given in the early months was to reorganise the headquarters, which was essentially the rudiment of an enriched NATO headquarters which by then had been totalled changed and had evolved into a huge mass of people that was not operating very effectively. And my assignment was to try, as quickly as possible, to form a headquarters to be transferred to Sarajevo, a small headquarters that would operate effectively to support the command of General Rose, and a small headquarters that would dedicate itself to personnel and materiel, logistics, from Split. In that month, in addition to other operations, we drafted a plan for the reorganisation and ensured that everybody working in the headquarters received a new job either in Sarajevo, or in Split, or at the three-sector headquarters that were simultaneously formed in Gornji Vakuf and in Sarajevo and in Tuzla. That was a very busy period in which some other incidents occurred, but we did succeed from 1 April in getting an operational small headquarters going in Sarajevo and in Split. From 1 April, I was in Sarajevo continuously, from where I travelled frequently the -- the travel designations included the UNPROFOR units throughout the area, also to Zagreb and to Split, but especially in Bosnia and Herzegovina to all the sites of the unit. I tried to visit them all to the extent permitted in the context of freedom of movement, and I also visited Pale sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, based on your last answer, it appears that you -- from the 1st of April, you were based in Sarajevo. Did you remain headquartered in Sarajevo throughout the rest of your tour in the theatre?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct, but I'd like to add that I did travel a lot across Bosnia-Herzegovina, and also to Bihac, and went to Zagreb and Split. So I did not spend 24/7 in Sarajevo, but that was the base from where I performed my duties as chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just to talk for a moment about your duties and responsibilities as chief of staff, could you outline for us what those were?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: First, the duty of the chief of staff was to ensure, together with the staff, that the commander had adequate support, received correct advice, and the moment decisions had been taken, that the correct orders were issued to have those duties performed. That's the work of the staff, as, in military terms, they're in support of the commander. Carrying out the mandate mainly entailed ensuring freedom of movement, ensuring that conditions were created to achieve a lasting cease-fire, and a third task was explicitly that aid organisations, such as UNHCR and others, be given the opportunity to perform their humanitarian duty. And a lot of this involves ensuring that the humanitarian relief items reached their destination in Bosnia at all sides of the confrontation lines. Second, we ensured that the injured could be treated among the civilians who had suffered deeply up to that point, and we also ensured that any injured were evacuated as needed, and that the quality of life of the people was improved, in part, by organising housing projects, and also, for example, by supplying plastic to insulate houses and seal them so that where a lot of destruction of doors and windows had taken place, people could, nonetheless, live. The staff supported all these activities, first of all, by trying to guarantee throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina that freedom of movement prevailed. All three parties had guaranteed this. In practice, however, the parties did not observe the freedom of movement agreements, and throughout my period there, that was the most serious problem. In May and June, we managed to ensure passage for nearly 100 per cent of the convoys, but after that the situation deteriorated, with all the consequences in 1995, both humanitarian relief and the supply of the military units in Sarajevo, and the other safe areas virtually ground to a halt. Another issue that was very important in that period was that we would get a clear picture of exactly what was happening on the ground throughout the area, and UNPROFOR -- a clear impression of what was happening on the ground. UNPROFOR was an impartial organisation. That meant that we did not have actual information that you need to do your work properly. We depended heavily on the information that we received from the warring parties. We depended heavily on the reports -- the reports from the UN Military Observers, and we depended heavily on the UNPROFOR units in the confrontation line or near the confrontation line, obtaining signals of what actually happened. But as for our own information organisation, we didn't have that, so we had to make do with the information made available to us. And in many cases, it was impossible to get a truly-confirmed impression, except through asking a lot of questions and trying to use the limited means that we had to confirm what was actually happening, and many of the reports went unconfirmed because they were unilateral reports from the warring parties. But we had virtually no opportunity to review them because we weren't allowed to review and check them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I just stop you there for a while, and I'd like to come back to some aspects of this. But to go to the beginning of your answer, you referred to the humanitarian relief and supply of military units in Sarajevo and other safe areas virtually grinding to a halt after May and June, and I note that paragraph 68 of your written evidence refers to a similar situation. There, you noted -- and I see you flipping through a document, General. Is that, by any chance, a copy of your statement?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 68 of your evidence, you noted that: "After June, the Bosnian Serbs placed very stringent restrictions on freedom of movement of UNPROFOR and aid convoys; for example, asking for more details of our movement, longer periods of notice, wanting to search our vehicles." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: I have that paragraph in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I would encourage you to listen to my questions. I'd like to ask you a little bit about your assertions in this paragraph. Were convoys -- when you say that convoys were ground to a halt, were they actually refused?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Increasingly from June, the convoys were refused, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How did that come about?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Well, the underlying motives that led Milovanovic either to provide verbal feedback, or through one of his staff or officers, that the convoys were refused were various, and I don't have any impression of the underlying motives, but I do of the arguments provided, and these often related to things such as the requests are tardy, or they're not properly substantiated, or there's no reason to carry out this convoy, or the request may be timely and substantiated, but you have requested the wrong route, at this time it's not convenient, we don't have the manpower to inspect. And then a great number of accusations towards UNPROFOR, where motives were used, such as: the convoys are intended to smuggle contraband into the enclaves, they're being used to transport weapons and munitions for the Muslims, they're being used to conduct illegal trade, or it's not necessary because the supplies for the units are still sufficient or the supplies for UNHCR in the enclaves are sufficient, and a great many accusations that I won't repeat here, but that concerned how people viewed the Muslim population in the enclaves. They were highly ingenious in coming up with constant new reasons for refusing the convoys. We did always ensure that the convoys didn't leave in the direction of the confrontation lines before we received confirmation that the convoys were, indeed, allowed. In addition, a great number of convoys were admitted or were admitted in part, but in May and April it turned out that a lot of convoys encountered measures -- they were subject to measures were not agreed. The convoys were scrutinised in the inspections, and the people accompanying the convoys had items, such as cameras and weapons, taken from them. And there's a large -- long list of items that were removed without any substantiation whatsoever, and UNPROFOR was not in a position to prevent this from happening. In most cases, they simply accepted these items being seized, hoping that the convoy would, nonetheless, be allowed to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You referred, in your answer, to allegations to the effect that UNPROFOR was smuggling contraband, transporting weapons and ammunition, and engaging in illegal trade. Did you -- on receiving these allegations, did you or your office conduct any investigations in that regard?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: UNHCR and other affiliated organisations are UN organisations and are supposed to work impartially and should not accept contraband for smuggling in any way, shape, or form. We had no reason whatsoever to inspect UNHCR convoys in advance to see whether anything was wrong. I'm convinced that if a convoy would have been inspected at a check-point and weapons and munition or other contraband were found there, that we certainly would have been given the opportunity to see this with our own eyes. I was never requested to visit such a situation on site, and I'm fully convinced that such a situation never occurred. The same holds true for the supply convoys sent to the units in the enclaves or to Sarajevo that were verbally accused of smuggling. There was never any moment when anybody from UNPROFOR was called to come to a check-point to take cognizance of a demonstrable smuggling incident. And I repeatedly broached the issue of such an invitation in my conversations with Milovanovic. I asked him, If you really see that there's something wrong, please call upon me and show it to me. But I never received any such invitation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your indulgence for just a moment. You also referred, in your answer at page 12, to the effect that convoys were -- encountered measures en route, were scrutinised in their inspections -- sorry, were scrutinised in the inspections, and the people accompanying the convoys had items, such as cameras and weapons, taken from them. Now, in that regard, I'd like to turn to a document. This is 65 ter 22987, and I should note, Your Honours, this is one of the proposed new documents we submitted in our notification requesting leave that it be added to our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that there's no opposition from the Defence, we'll admit it -- we'll grant it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have 65 ter 22987, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, do you see the document on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Yes. [In English] Yes, I see a letter from me to General Mladic. [Interpretation] Dated 28 June 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, General, this letter, did you have an opportunity to look at it in preparation for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall, actually, writing this letter, General?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: I remember that, and I also remember that there was virtually no response or no response at all. There's an annex that goes with this letter, and the annex reflects a complete chart of all the material taken away from UNPROFOR units. And to my knowledge, nothing was returned, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we then go to page 2 of this document to see the annex.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, on page 2, in the fourth paragraph from the top, you see the notation that says: "Since the beginning of May, the BSA -" I assume referring to the Bosnian Serb Army - "have hardened their position concerning the inspection of UN convoys in the territory." Now, does this accurately reflect the situation you've described in your earlier answers?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct. In my contacts with General Milovanovic, it was repeatedly mentioned that he believed that more stringent inspection was necessary. Excuse me, no, that more stringent inspection was necessary on the territory of the Serbs -- not that he believed. But in addition to that more stringent inspection, nonetheless, many things happened that were unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that this be marked as the next Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1819, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You referred earlier on in your answers, General, to a deterioration of the situation and, similarly, a deterioration of the situation in terms of freedom of movement, and I wonder if you could tell us whether these -- to your knowledge, whether these restrictions on freedom of movement had any effect on the situation in the eastern enclaves.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: As I stated earlier, in May and June Bosnia-Herzegovina Command managed to bring the humanitarian convoys to a very high acceptable level. From June, that plummeted once again, and the consequence was that, during the fall and winter and spring of 1995, the situation in the enclaves, both among the civilians and among the UNPROFOR present, became extremely desperate. Bosnia-Herzegovina Command had a system of tracking the quantity of supplies in the enclave, both humanitarian and for the UNPROFOR units, and you can tell that the situation is becoming very desperate, because in February and March there is a mild surge and then suddenly it became dramatic in the run-up to the fall of Srebrenica enclave. We can only guess at the reason behind this, but one of the points that we had was that there was a systematic squeeze-out of the opportunities to function properly, militarily, for the UNPROFOR units in the enclave. In addition, the situation for the civilian population became increasingly desperate as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps, given your -- now that we've moved on to 1995, I could show you a couple of documents in that regard. Could we have 65 ter 03673, please. That's a document dated 7 April 1995 from General Milovanovic to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and the Drina Corps Commands. I'll just --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may make an observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Defence, this is a completely new approach, that General Van Baal is going to talk about the events following August 1994. We counted on him dealing with the period that he was there, that is, until September 1994. Having said that, we would need additional time to prepare ourselves for that. There is nothing in the statement or the identification of 65 ter documents, so this is a completely new and untackled subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We know he was posted until August 1994, and we'll see what he has to say about the events in 1995. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This, as I said earlier, is a document dated 7 April 1995 from the VRS Main Staff to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and the Drina Corps Commands, informing them that the Main Staff had not approved movement of a number of convoys and teams. Now, General, did you have an opportunity to review this document in preparation for your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Well, yes, I was able to peruse this, although it was a new document for me. I did not see this document in 1995. I saw it recently, in preparations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to take you to page 2 of the English version of this document, item number 9, which refers to a convoy from Kiseljak which was supposed to transport diesel fuel to Srebrenica, and then over to page 3, please. I'll give you moment to look at item 9.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: [In English] I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then over to page 3, please, item number 10, which refers to a convoy from Kiseljak which is supposed to transport field beds, hospital beds, and other things to Srebrenica. Now, General, do you see the last line of this document before the signature block, which reads: "Inform the check-points of the above, and if any of the convoys come to the crossings, you know the procedure"? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do see that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I noted, General, in your written evidence at paragraph 69, you said that: "The conditions set out by General Milovanovic of the Main Staff were imposed by individuals at check-points." Do you see any relationship between your observations in your written evidence and the procedures and directions as set out in this document?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: There are great parallels, and in my experiences of 1994, as chief of staff, and how it was linked back to me that convoys were refused, and what conduct was at the check-points, and this was relayed to me by commanders of DutchBat 2 and 3 at the time that I had returned to Holland and I was director of operations in the Dutch military, the information in the UN channels also ends up in the national channels and, and there are great similarities between what I experienced in 1994 and that which my successors experienced and also commanders of DutchBat 2 and 3 in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this document refers to a convoy being refused which was supposed to transport diesel fuel to Srebrenica. That was at point number 9 of this document. To your knowledge, were the UN forces in Srebrenica in 1995 affected by lack of fuel?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Well, actually, one of the main tasks of Bosnia-Herzegovina Command was to give truly accurate situation descriptions of the situations in which the UNPROFOR units and the population had ended up in, both in the safe areas and in other areas in Bosnia. And that means that also in Holland we followed very closely the position of supplies, how many supplies there were in the enclave, and what was interesting for Holland were, of course, DutchBat 3 stores in Srebrenica. And really after the final convoy, as I recall, in February 1995, that's when the situation deteriorated very rapidly, and it became necessary that DutchBat 3 started using the supplies of UNHCR to be able to function at all, at an absolute minimum level. And at a given point in that period, stores and supplies of fuel were reduced almost to nil. The only fuel that remained was wood on which we could try and cook food. And there was very little left to keep the hospital going. But almost everything else was done on foot, with minimal vehicle activity, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm looking at the witness summary for General Van Baal, and I don't see any reference to the events in Srebrenica. And I think if he's going to testify about those events, we would ask that his cross-examination be postponed until sometime next year, when we deal with the Srebrenica events, because we're not prepared to deal with that on cross-examination. We have no notice that his testimony would be dealing with those events. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to respond, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a couple of things. The documents we're referring to were part of our initial notification with respect to this witness. The only new document, we've already dealt with, and that was a letter generated by General Van Baal, himself. So we're not dealing with any documents that were by way of surprise to the Defence. With respect to the issues we're going into -- and I should note my line of questioning is strictly related to the freedom of movement of convoys and humanitarian aid -- those areas were discussed with the witness in proofing yesterday and notified at the earliest possible opportunity to the Defence, which, because of our time constraints that we're all operating under, was late yesterday afternoon. But I would oppose the cross-examination going into next year or, indeed, being delayed at all in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just respond very briefly. This document that we're looking at, for one, doesn't deal at all with Srebrenica, so I don't think that we had any notice, at least for this particular document, that there would be testimony about Srebrenica events. And we don't object if they want to elicit that kind of testimony, and the general is local here, so it shouldn't be any inconvenience for him to come back for cross-examination, but we don't think that we should be required to cross-examination on -- cross-examine on part of the case which we're not prepared for and which we had no notice this witness would deal with. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You wouldn't oppose the witness dealing with item number 9 on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, with respect to this document, I don't think this is a proper document to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm only dealing with it in terms of notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: In terms of notice, we've had notice of this document, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber notes the extent of questions relating to Srebrenica in relation to this witness is somewhat limited, and at a later stage, if the Defence is able to show good cause to recall this witness, the Chamber will consider the matter at the time. We'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to ask that this document, please, be marked at this point as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. We'd like to object to the use of this document. I think this is a very slippery slope for both the Prosecution and the Defence, to take a document that comes from a different time, when the witness was present, and simply say, This is somehow consistent with what I was experiencing. If we start doing that, we could have, let's say, a Defence witness talking about 1992, and show him all kinds of documents for the rest of the war to say this is consistent, this is consistent, and then it becomes an open door to admit evidence which is really not very probative. I note that General Milovanovic is a Prosecution witness, he'll be testifying here, and I think he would be the more appropriate witness through whom to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to respond, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the jurisprudence on pattern evidence applies squarely in this case. This document is relevant to show a consistent pattern. The general has already been able to draw parallels between the situation as he experienced it in 1994 with regard to freedom of movement and effective control of the freedom of movement of humanitarian aid to the enclaves, and I would submit it's clearly relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Clearly, the witness was able to see there was some parallel in this document to what was happening while he was posted there. But in the Chamber's view, it does not appear that the witness had referred to this document, as such. So separate from the issue whether you can tender this through a Bar Table motion, the Chamber does not find it appropriate to admit this through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, referring to your written evidence at paragraph 61, page 15, you -- and relating to an incident in April 1994, you said that even after one and a half months, you had the strong conviction that all UNPROFOR movements on VRS areas were tightly controlled. Have you found that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What do you base that on?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That paragraph is in front of me, I'm sorry. I based myself on various incidents that occurred in that period where, at a time when there was contact with headquarters, the VRS, we also noticed that the agreements that we could make there were actually being followed up.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you have any personal experience in that regard, when you refer to various incidents?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Yes. I can mention three examples. The first is: The non-authorised weapons in the environment of Citluk, Crnici [as interpreted], and the activities that UNPROFOR engaged in to bring those weapons under UNPROFOR control. In the night, remote-control mines were placed under the vehicles of the Canadian Forces, and at the moment that these were referred to with the headquarters of the VRS, they assured us that these would be removed, and they were removed. However, at the next moment they were replaced there, placed back there. And, secondly, in personal contact in Pale with the officials involved, once again the assignment was given to remove those remote-controlled mines, and this did, in fact, happen within 20 minutes. That's the first example. The second example is the time at which I wanted to do an investigation into the incident with a British soldier who was killed in a fire-fight in Gorazde, and I was at the check-point in Rogatica, I was confronted with Captain Zoran. He was being instructed based on a facsimile, a message, in which it was stated precisely that the convoy, which consisted of two vehicles, should submit to a search, with the exception of the -- of General Van Baal and his personal effects. This was a fax message that was read out exactly to state what assignment had -- what order had to be executed. And the third was a time at which NAVO [as interpreted] had unauthorised weapons systems taken away from weapons collection points around Sarajevo, that those weapons systems would be attacked with NATO air attacks, and I, in any case, in due consultation with General Rose, agreed that it was not our intention to kill any personnel there, simply just to obliterate the arms systems. And in direct contact with the liaisons officer in Lukavica Barracks, a Major Indjic, I had a talk with him in which I pointed out to him that the unauthorised weapons systems would be attacked by NATO within a short period, and he had to make sure that all personnel -- all staff had been removed from the vicinity of these unauthorised weapons. And he called me back within 10 or 15 minutes to tell me that that separation of equipment -- of materiel and personnel had actually been executed. These are only three examples in a list of many which I won't all repeat. Then I would really need my notes from that period, I would need to peruse my reports from that time, but these are just three illustrative -- three illustrations from which I concluded that what was decided to be done at Pijeseko [phoen] Pale or to not do were things that were actually being followed up on on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In your experience and your involvement with the Dutch Battalion in UNPROFOR that followed your return to the theatre, did you see anything to -- that might alter this conviction that you held to the effect that all UNPROFOR movements on VRS areas were tightly controlled?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: It confirmed the impression I had acquired in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Those are my questions, Your Honours, for the examination-in-chief. There just remains to deal with the matter of associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we deal with them right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I note, from the additional exhibits, Your Honour, we've only sought to tender one from that list, which has been admitted. That was 65 ter 22987.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And why don't we come to the issue of associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are some documents that have been already admitted through other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. I've discussed this with my colleague. One identified as 65 ter 11570 is Exhibit P969.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And you also listed other -- exhibits that have been already exhibited -- admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's just for reference purposes?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, quite so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One item, the second-last item, the 65 ter number of which is 32735, your explanation is that is intercepted conversation between General Van Baal and Milovanovic, but you said -- referred to para 76, but para 76 refers to the intercept between General Van Baal and Mr. Karadzic. I don't think this is the proper one. So you would like to --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Please, let me look into that, Your Honour, and address you on it as quickly as possible. I'm sure you're correct, and my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection from the Defence, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just with respect to the prior witness statement and the transcripts of the testimony, I don't know if the Prosecution is minded to tender those, but we don't normally have them tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it is their intention. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I really apologise to Your Honours that I seem to have -- I do this from time to time. The 65 ter number which is listed as 32727 should actually read "32737." And I'm very sorry about that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So except for those items referred to, will be admitted and given numbers. Just shall I go through one by one? So except for 32735 and all the other items that have been already admitted, and except for those statements referred to by Mr. Robinson, will be admitted and given numbers. Mr. Karadzic, can you start your cross-examination now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General. I'm sorry that you did not have any communication with the Defence and we have to finalise things that we could have finalised in an interview of that nature. The objective or the intention of the Defence is not to dispute, or to subject you to scrutiny, or test the conduct of the UN or of different countries, or you, personally. We just want to talk about erroneously-established facts. In that sense, I noticed that you made reference today to your notes. That would be very helpful for us in order to bridge the gap over the years that have elapsed and to rectify, possibly, any mistakes that might occur in the perception. Is it possible that you make these notes of yours accessible to us?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: I don't see any reason whatsoever to release them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, in that case, I have to ask assistance from the Trial Chamber in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic. It's for you to make submission, if necessary. Before you move on: Ms. Edgerton, there's one thing I forgot to raise. It's related to 65 ter 21862, which is a part of General Milovanovic's personal diary. I take it that you are tendering only three pages that was referred to by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At this moment, yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In order for us to be able to establish more precisely and clarify certain things, let me ask you: General, do you know that we gave consent to the presence of UN forces in our country?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: UNPROFOR was able to act, at the consent of the three former warring parties, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you then accept that we were one of the equal warring parties?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: To UNPROFOR, all parties were equal. We were impartial and non-combatant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you accept that, in compliance with International Laws of War and the Geneva Conventions, we enjoyed identical rights as the other two warring factions?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: To the United Nations, all three parties were equivalent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to your experience, were we treated equally by the international community, the UN and its agencies?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: It's not up to me, in my position here, to pass judgement about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to your experience, as did my learned friend Ms. Edgerton. But if you do not wish to answer this question, let us move on. Did you treat us equally as the other two parties or one of the parties that was our opponent? I'm talking about you, personally, as well as your command.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: You're the best person to judge that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, do you accept that as a party that had to pass through -- relief and humanitarian aid through its territory, we were entitled to establish the rules under which these convoys of humanitarian aid would be treated and how it would be delivered and distributed?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Very generally, back in 1993 the military commanders, including on the Serb side, reached an agreement with UNPROFOR to allow the convoys to pass without hindrance. And the practice, as I experienced in 1994, was that particularly the Serb side kept imposing new restrictions, either to prevent the convoys from proceeding, or to seriously delay them, or to cancel them altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, General, that you were always being given the reasons and the basis on which a convoy was either halted or denied passage?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, we were always given reasons why that was the case, but the reasons were not valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you accept that the Serb side had their own perception of their safety and security, and that it was -- security-related issues were something that was up to the Serb side to decide?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That was, in effect, the situation. And UNPROFOR's mandate did not allow us to change that by force, so we just had to live with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to remind you of the Additional Protocol to the Geneva Conventions, which refers to civilians in wartime. That's the 4th Geneva Convention of 1949, Article 23 in Chapter 2. If you wish, I can give you a hard copy, or perhaps we can call up 1D2612, so just that you can take a brief look at what the International Law guarantees to us. 1D2612. This is page 1. General, you see the title there. Can we please now have page 9. I'd like you and the others to focus on Article 23, and specifically sub-items A, B and C, all the way through to Article 24. I'm not going to read it, but I am kindly asking you to go through it. Do you notice that the party allowing humanitarian aid to pass through has the right to impose conditions, and that serious reasons proffered by that party should not be taken as something to be benefitted by the other party?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That corresponds very generally with how it reads here, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that you, yourself, pointed out that the situation with the passage of convoys differs at times? There were periods when it all ran smoothly; on the other hand, there were periods when there was heightened inspection, and there was a high level of dissatisfaction on the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: As I have already stated, in May and June the humanitarian convoys were largely allowed to proceed, including the resupply convoy for the UNPROFOR units in the safe areas. Afterwards, this changed drastically and became subject to rigid regulations that did not correspond with the 25 November 1993 agreement concerning freedom of movement that was the foundation for the agreements between the warring parties and UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you cast your mind back at the consumption of ammunition by UNPROFOR units in, let's say, enclaves?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: What is your question, if I may?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is: What was the level of monthly consumption of ammunition by your units posted in the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Very limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You didn't shoot much, did you?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: There was no reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, what was, then, the reason for your asking for additional supplies of the ammunition, and consequently you were receiving this ammunition in the enclave, given that you say that you were not using it?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: First, part of the munition was used, to the extent possible, for practice. Second, it's necessary for munition that requires extensive operations and is retrieved from and reinserted into weapons, it needs to be replaced. In addition, there's quality care, that certain types of munition actually have to be replaced every half year or year because maintenance is required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I note the time. If it is convenient, we'll have a break now. We'll have a break for 20 minutes and resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just address you for a moment on the two outstanding items from the list of associated exhibits. That's the intercept at 65 ter 32737, dated 23 July 1994, between General Van Baal and Milovanovic, and of course Your Honour was quite correct, 32734, rather than 32735, an intercepted conversation between General Van Baal and General Milovanovic. Those are properly up-loaded in e-court now, Your Honours, and I wonder if I might ask they be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The intercepted conversation between General Van Baal and General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was reading from the document. General Van Baal and Dr. Karadzic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And that's 65 ter 32734?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you suggested marking them for identification?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Given that they were transcripts, rather than audios, I thought marking for identification would be -- was the practice we had been following, actually, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that the general is a participant in that conversation, is it not a proper time to authenticate that transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May they be marked as Prosecution exhibits, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no opposition from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We maintain our previous position, but we understand you've been admitting these when the participant is here as a witness. But we maintain our objection to the lawfulness and, under Rule 95, we continue to object to intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is my understanding that the Defence has no opposition [Realtime transcript read in error "position"] as to the admission of intercepts during the wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, are you trying to say that you conducted exercises with combat ammunition in the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: In any case, there was some limited exercising with small arms and ammunition, to maintain our ability to shoot at targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you accept that this had to have disturbed the Serbian soldiers around the enclaves, if firing was heard in the enclave? Did you inform the Serbian Army that you would be conducting an exercise?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: To my knowledge, that was agreed locally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you then accept that the quantities of ammunition that UNPROFOR was bringing into the enclaves each time were cause for suspicion on our part? I'm speaking about perception. Do you accept that the perception on the other side was that this could have been misused or would be misused?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: I would, in fact, say the opposite and say that arrangements were made from the outset to develop units in the enclaves that had to manage independently for a certain period, and in that respect it cannot be presumed in advance that a huge war machine would be built up but that a unit, in the event of self-defence, might actually be able to protect itself, and that requires a certain quantity of munition as well as other supplies. And that was discussed extensively in advance during this build-up of the units in Srebrenica and Gorazde and one other place, Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, how frequently did the UNPROFOR have supply convoys coming into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Basically, co-ordinated with this build-up and the switching off of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How frequently did you request supply convoys to bring in ammunition into the enclave, large quantities of ammunition? Was that once a month, twice a month? How frequent was this?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: The build-up of the unit in Srebrenica, as well as the build-up of the unit in Gorazde, took several months. And I can't repeat, off the top of my head at this point, how often munition appeared on the waybill. I can't repeat that off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you were to hand your notes over to us, then it would be clearer. But, General, tell me this: Were you able to build up your military presence in the enclaves without our agreement?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you seek this agreement from us?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Continuously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we are going to see how this was reflected in one of your conversations with General Milovanovic, where he is informing you why a convoy was stopped, because it was announced that a relief of the forces would be brought in, but no forces that were relieved would actually leave the enclave, in order to build up the strength in the enclave, which was not acceptable. Were there such instances, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: I don't have any opinion about this without date, time, and a specific report in front of me. All I can do is speculate, and I won't do that. I would like to ask Mr. Karadzic to indicate exactly with a document or transcript referring to such an instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to call up a document now. General, sir, can you please tell me if you accept that we had the right to inspect the convoys that we were allowing to pass through?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: The general right to inspect a convoy was never contested, but in many cases we couldn't even carry out the convoys because they were rejected in advance in many cases after June, and so they never departed and never reached the Serb check-points either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, everything that came into the enclaves came with the consent of the Serbian side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that ammunition, fuel, and other items were smuggled, and the United Nations were even conducting investigations into these matters?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: From the period in which I was there, I have not found any evidence of such investigations being conducted, nor any confirmations that UNPROFOR/UNHCR units were smuggling goods into the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of investigations relating to the black market and that it was established that certain lower-ranking soldiers, probably without the knowledge of their commands, participated in the creation of a black market?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: I did not see any evidence on paper or personally, based on the presence in the enclave. I never found anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that when a convoy is approved, the soldiers at the check-point must pay attention that everything is the way it is stated in the papers? So if something is there that is undeclared, they don't have the authority or the discretion to deviate from items that are not declared? For example, if, instead of 10 trucks, 11 trucks appear, isn't it to be assumed that a soldier at the check-point cannot approve the passage of such a convoy?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: The convoys had a waybill. We agreed with the Serb authorities what had to be indicated on the waybill, and the contents had to be limited to that. That's what we agreed. But, in any case, that was often not the reason to block the convoy from proceeding. I repeat that most convoys were rejected after they were requested. And in one instance, there was a dispute at a check-point because something wasn't right on the waybill or load manifest, but that was an exception.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, you have one attitude towards General Milovanovic, who was your counterpart, the chief of staff, just like you, and then in your conversations with him and in documents that you exchanged, it can be seen that there was mutual respect and good co-operation. So how do you explain this difference in your statements? Your position is quite against the Serbs and General Milovanovic, but at that time the atmosphere or the tone in your relations, and the co-operation between you, was quite good, it was better.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: During the period I was there, there was some moments when we had serious differences of opinion. The most important one was the attitude and the refusal to allow convoys, and this greatly threatened the proper functioning of UNPROFOR. So it's not my call to say that this relationship was disturbed, but it was clearly disturbed in that the agreements we reached when we saw each other or spoke to each other over the phone were not observed or were observed insufficiently by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D2655 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I feel a little better now that I see that the Muslim authorities did not only eavesdrop on my conversations, but they also eavesdropped on yours. So this is a report by the Bosnia and Herzegovina MUP, the Security Department. This is 2655. If we don't have a translation, just allow me to summarise what this document is. It's this: You spoke on the 20th of May, 1994, with the assistance of an interpreter, Ms. X. And then in the second paragraph -- actually, this was a conversation of yours with General Milovanovic. In the second paragraph -- I don't need to read everything. In the second paragraph, it says: "The second question has to do with the --" And this is you speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We seem to have an English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's on the way, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be much easier if, in the disclosed material, we were also given the translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, how frequently did you call General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Very regularly; sometimes three times a day, sometimes once a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are going to get the document in a second, but I'm going to interpret this. You will be able to read it later. So you were asking for convoys for Gorazde. The first convoy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's four pages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the first page, please. [In English] "The second issue ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we zoom in on the lower part. Yes. Can you read, General, or shall we zoom in a bit further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it can be concluded, on the basis of this paragraph, that you were aware of our right to carry out inspections as we saw fit and dictated by our suspicions?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Checking on the load manifest was an agreement that we had made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I now ask you: In the next paragraph, where we can see that General Milovanovic is asking for an investigation to be conducted into the murder of a Ukrainian soldier - when you finish the paragraph, just let us know and then we'll look at the next page - where we can see that General Milovanovic is requesting a multi-level investigative commission, believing that unilateral investigation results should not be accepted, and we see that he's interested in the truth, and he promises that if this deed was committed by a Serb, the Serb would be punished. Can you please let us know if you see that on this page. This is the fourth paragraph, which says: "I care about the truth, and only about the truth ..." And so on and so forth. And he's asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we go down further. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you agree here, but you said that your commander has the final word in this, and the same applies to the other side. And then Milovanovic, in the last paragraph at the bottom, is informing you that he received another one of your requests for the police to go to the scene for an investigation. Can we look at the next page, please. Top of the page, please. It seems to me, General, sir, that this is a pleasant relationship, full of mutual requests, and not one that you seem to present in your statements. Is that correct? And at the bottom, we see that two convoys were authorised because of you, personally, General. That's what it says. "... only for the general, personally." Is that correct, and do you confirm the contents of this intercept?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember the literal text. I'm confronted with this for the first time. But I do recall this situation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the next page. Is it correct that these announcements were arriving at the last minute always, even immediately before, so that the requests for convoys to be let through were sent at the last minute? Can you please answer that question, and then we can move to the text.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: The fact that -- I'm sorry, I can't hear -- that they were dispatched at a very late moment, I cannot confirm that. Generally, very stringent measures were always taken to make sure that what had to take place was in accordance with agreements that had been made in the number of days and hours before a convoy started out. I believe there was a technical problem with sending the applications at one time, because they were going through UNMO Pale, the United Nations Military Observers in Pale, who had to send it through to headquarters in Pale, and so there may have been disturbances in the smooth transition here and there, I cannot rule that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you see in the second paragraph that General Milovanovic is concerned because he doesn't see a unit coming out after a unit is allowed in, and so he's talking about this unauthorised reinforcement of forces, and then he says at the end that's the reason why the second convoy was not authorised. And then you thank him, and the rest of it is like a joke or like a pleasant conversation. Do you agree that General Milovanovic, just like General Mladic and the rest of the Army of Republika Srpska's main concern was not to be defeated, so they did not want to make that possible by not approving the convoys?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: This is -- this is your own interpretation, but very emphatically in the situation of the run-off at Gorazde, we made an agreement with the UNPROFOR units as to their enhancement. It included the numbers of troops that would be allowed to conduct their duties there. That is nothing new. Also, with the earlier warring factions, this had been an agreement about exactly what would happen, how this would take place. And Mr. Karadzic's remark as to the second part of this paragraph I would just simply leave to his own account.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we tender this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D819, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What I asked you about, the duties and the obligations of General Milovanovic, you, as a general, is it your main concern to protect your troops from getting killed and to avoid being defeated?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That is a responsibility that we had. UNPROFOR had to create circumstances that would facilitate a lasting cease-fire. There were several ways to do that, but always with the joint approvement of the earlier warring factions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that on the Serb side, there was the perception and even evidence that after each convoy that entered an enclave, the Muslim side would step up its attacks from within those enclaves, so would you agree that this was a cause for concern on the Serbian part in relation to the convoys?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Convoys were supplying UNPROFOR. These were the military ones. But the humanitarian ones were mainly for the civilian population and had nothing to do with the possible strengthening of Muslim military capacity in the enclave. In my period, UNPROFOR convoys and UNHCR convoys or other affiliated agency convoys would also -- would never include military goods for the civilian population inside the enclave. The Muslim population, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will show you. You will see evidence that this actually did happen. But, actually, can we now look at 1D2656, how permissions were sought at the last minute and how General Milovanovic was very understanding. 1D2656. Again, the Muslim side was eavesdropping on General Milovanovic and you. And may I ask if there is a translation for this document as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Its translation is coming, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Here it is, also four pages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the translation on the ELMO, please. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the first sentence, where it says: "General --" Actually, General Milovanovic speaks of you, and he says: "General Van Baal thinks that I'm his secretary. He's been calling me the whole day." And then you say: "General, sometimes we have the same interests, so I have to call you." And then Milovanovic says you should talk to each other once in 10 days and not 15 times a day. And then if you look at the bottom, you are asking: "All right, General, thank you for that ..." And then you ask -- you say that at 6.00 that evening, Mr. De Mello informed you about this, and you're actually asking that a convoy that was not announced sufficiently in advance, you're kindly asking for this convoy to be allowed through that evening, and General Milovanovic says: "No problem, they will be allowed to pass through, but I have to receive the fax or you need to give me their names." And then the image we get of General Milovanovic, on the basis of your statements, is much worse than the image that we get on the basis of your conversations with him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpreters couldn't hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We respected each other in conversations, the way you should do if you're an impartial UNPROFOR party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, could you kindly take a look at the transcript and check whether some part of your answer is missing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The way I should do if you are an impartial UNPROFOR party." So not "we," but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you thinking only of your written correspondence or do you also include your telephone conversations here?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Well, there were a number of telephone conversations that were intercepted, that were listened to. I did see transcripts of those. And there were times at which we were not quite so respectful with each other, one time at which General Milovanovic told me that, Wasn't it wonderful that we hadn't killed each other on that specific day, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this was a joke, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Well, you've got to distinguish between moments at which General Milovanovic made jokes and at times that he did not make jokes, even if there was an intermediary in the form of an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And we can see that Milovanovic said that you went a bit too far with your demands, that you were giving him homework and asking him to do it, and he said that: "The only thing that is left, and I would be glad, and it is my wish to invite you to my headquarters here in Sarajevo, and if you could come by, any chance, I would like that to actually happen sometime." And then a little bit down, Milovanovic says: "This is what I told you. Pale was just a joke. Yes, I'll meet you in my territory any time. You're always welcome there. We'll see each other, of course, and now I have to work as fast as I can in regards to these three passengers that you did not announce, and you don't need to send me the fax ..." So, General, is this proof that General Milovanovic did his utmost to grant your requests, and that he wasn't being restrictive?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Again, the interpreters couldn't hear because of the switch in the system, can't hear at all now. We do apologise. Could he start again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There seems to have been a technical -- [Dutch language on English channel]. Yes, it seems to be resolved now. Repeat your last answer now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this situation, he did not conduct restrictively, but he behaved cooperatively.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have this document admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D820, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D2657, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is the English translation coming?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We have one, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, while we are waiting for the document, you can take my word for it this is, again, the Secret Service of the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or the State Security Department. It concerns your conversation with General Milovanovic of the 2nd of June, 1994. You greeted them by saying, Good evening, and the time is 20 past 10.00 in the evening. From the first paragraph, you can see that you have two questions. One concerns the convoy that was still in Rogatica, and the other one dealt with the deployment of your forces in Sarajevo. The British convoy in Rogatica, for the supply of their unit -- you can see this first paragraph, can't you? Now, let's see what General Milovanovic says in response: "Firstly, concerning the convoy stopped at Rogatica today, afternoon, I have issued the instructions to my personnel to let the convoy through. However, only a few lorries were checked, and a cheeky English officer wouldn't allow us to check the remaining vehicles. He wouldn't allow us to lift the tarpaulin over the top of the lorry. As for the bags with the mail, I can really suspect UNPROFOR is, indeed, delivering weapons and ammunition to the Muslims of Gorazde." And you say -- can we please have the next page, or just scroll up. You say: "General, I agree with you that we are dealing here with a routine and standard control, and, General, it is apparent that you and I are receiving different information from the field." And so on and so forth. Milovanovic then goes on to say -- can we please have the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: [In English] One moment, please. I have to read it. I see this for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Take your time, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And General Milovanovic says here: "I will instruct my men not to check those mail bags, but I beg you to instruct your personnel to remove the tarpaulin so that my men could check the cargo ..." And you say: "This is what I intend to do." Now, General, my question is as follows: Did the Serbian Army request these examinations because it was an evil army, bent on disturbing the process, or did they do this in compliance with the right that they had to conduct the inspections and their concerns about what the other side might have been receiving in that way? Were the Serbs evil or were they simply concerned?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only guess as to what was on the minds of the Serbs. What we had agreed was that there would be a visual inspection of the vehicles, but no searching, in the sense of no personal bodily searches or of the personal possessions of the people.
